name: Hasura GraphQL Engine
license: Apache 2.0 (server); Enterprise Edition and Hasura Cloud are commercial
summary: Hasura’s open-source v2 engine: point it at Postgres or another supported database and it serves a GraphQL API with queries, mutations and live subscriptions, guarded by role-based row and column permissions.
intro: The engine, written in Haskell, connects to one or more databases and generates a GraphQL schema from the tables, views and relationships you track, with filtering, sorting, pagination and aggregates. Each GraphQL request becomes a single SQL query that runs in the database, so nested reads don’t turn into one query per row. Permissions are declared per role, per table and per operation: a boolean filter over columns and session variables, such as `X-Hasura-User-Id` taken from a JWT or an auth webhook, plus the list of columns the role may see, and the engine writes them into that SQL query. Subscriptions come in two kinds. Live queries re-run a query on an interval and push changed results; the engine batches many subscribers with the same query into one SQL statement by passing their variables as rows, and Hasura’s benchmark held one million live queries with Postgres at about 28% load. Streaming subscriptions return only new rows. Around the generated API, Actions add custom logic through HTTP handlers, Remote Schemas merge other GraphQL APIs into one endpoint, Event Triggers call webhooks on inserts, updates and deletes, Scheduled Triggers run on a timer, and RESTified endpoints expose saved queries as REST. Configuration is metadata, managed through an API, the console or the CLI with migrations.

Postgres and compatible databases (including Citus and CockroachDB), SQL Server and BigQuery work in the open-source Community Edition; Snowflake, Amazon Athena, MySQL (in alpha), Oracle, MariaDB and MongoDB need Enterprise. The self-hosted Enterprise Edition adds query caching, read replicas, API limits, allow lists, multiple JWT secrets and OpenTelemetry export. Hasura Cloud runs the engine for you: Free allows 3 million requests and 100 MB of data passthrough a month, Professional removes the database and project limits and charges $0.13 per GB of passthrough, and Enterprise adds SSO, failover and VPC peering. Hasura DDN, built on a new Rust engine, is the company’s successor product, and since June 2025 its focus has been PromptQL; Hasura said the v2 engine would continue to be hosted and maintained, and it still ships releases, with 2.51.2 on 23 October 2026.
strengths: A full GraphQL API from an existing database with no resolvers to write, and one SQL query per request instead of N+1 queries
Row and column permissions as declarative rules that use session variables from your auth system
Live queries scale by batching many subscribers into one SQL statement, so realtime UIs don’t need a separate change feed
Actions, Remote Schemas and Event Triggers add business logic and side effects without forking the engine
limits: No longer Hasura’s main product: the company’s focus moved to DDN and then PromptQL, and v2 is maintained rather than promoted, though it still gets regular releases
Live queries poll the database on an interval and refetch whole results, which adds latency when writes are rare
Feature support varies by database: BigQuery has no mutations or subscriptions, event triggers work only on Postgres and SQL Server, and several databases need Enterprise
Caching, read replicas, API limits and OpenTelemetry need Enterprise Edition or Hasura Cloud

story: Hasura first added GraphQL to the data APIs of its Kubernetes platform, then pulled it out as a standalone product. The open-source GraphQL Engine launched on 10 July 2018 with “instant realtime GraphQL APIs on a Postgres database”, using about 50 MB of RAM, and in August 2018 any query could be turned into a subscription.

Hasura 2.0, released on 23 February 2021, connected several databases to one instance at once, added SQL Server and BigQuery, created REST endpoints from GraphQL templates, extended authorization to remote GraphQL services and added metadata APIs and a maintenance mode for upgrades.

In June 2023 Hasura announced the Data Delivery Network with a v3 engine rewritten in Rust, and on 2 June 2025 it made PromptQL its focus, saying the GraphQL Engine and DDN would continue to be hosted and maintained. The v2 server kept receiving releases through 2026.

choices.choice: Compile each GraphQL request into one SQL query
choices.why: Resolving fields one by one would send many small queries to the database. Compiling the whole request, permissions included, lets Postgres plan it once.

choices.choice: Poll and batch live queries instead of listening for changes
choices.why: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY can drop events and logical replication slots are costly or unavailable on managed databases, so the engine refetches on an interval and batches subscribers; the stated trade-off is latency when writes are few.
A permission is a boolean expression plus a column list, so the engine can put it into the generated SQL and the same rules apply to queries, mutations and subscriptions.
Hasura 2.0 made configuration API-driven so tools could manage changes, inspect them and move them between environments.

timeline.text: GraphQL Engine launches for Postgres in July; subscriptions in August
Hasura 2.0: multiple databases, SQL Server, BigQuery, REST endpoints
Hasura DDN and a Rust v3 engine announced
Company focus moves to PromptQL; v2 to be maintained
